title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile

hero.subtitle: The PKI framework that underpins digital trust on the Internet, defining the format for digital certificates used in TLS, code signing, and email security.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
X.509 certificates bind a public key to an identity through a chain of trust. Certificate Authorities (CAs) issue and sign certificates, allowing relying parties to verify the identity of servers, clients, and other entities.

Every HTTPS connection you make relies on X.509 certificates to verify you're talking to the intended server and not an impersonator.
sections.eli5: Anyone can claim to be a website. A certificate is like a passport: a trusted office checked who you are and stamped it, so others can believe you.

sections.title: Certificate Format
sections.content:
An X.509 v3 certificate contains several fields encoded in ASN.1 DER format:

Versionv3 (value 2) for modern certificates
Serial NumberUnique identifier assigned by the CA
Signature AlgorithmAlgorithm used by the CA to sign (e.g., sha256WithRSAEncryption)
IssuerDistinguished Name of the issuing CA
ValiditynotBefore and notAfter dates
SubjectDistinguished Name of the certificate holder
Subject Public Key InfoThe public key and its algorithm
Extensionsv3 extensions like Subject Alternative Name, Key Usage, etc.
sections.eli5: The card has labelled boxes: whose it is, who stamped it, when it runs out, and the secret-lock half that anyone may use to send them private mail.

sections.title: Certificate Path Validation
sections.content:
To verify a certificate, the relying party must build and validate a certification path from the end-entity certificate to a trusted root CA.

Chain Building
Follow issuer references from end-entity up to a trusted root
Signature Verification
Each certificate's signature is verified using the issuer's public key
Validity Checking
Current time must fall within each certificate's validity period
Revocation Checking
Check CRLs or OCSP responders for revoked certificates
sections.eli5: To trust a card, you check the stamp, then check who made that stamp, and keep going until you reach someone you already trust. You also check nothing has expired or been cancelled.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
X.509 v3 extensions provide additional identity information and constraints:

Subject Alternative NameDNS names, IPs, emails the cert covers
Key UsagedigitalSignature, keyEncipherment, etc.
Extended Key UsageserverAuth, clientAuth, codeSigning
Basic ConstraintsWhether this cert can act as a CA
Authority Key IdentifierIdentifies the issuing CA's key
CRL Distribution PointsURLs for Certificate Revocation Lists
sections.eli5: Extra lines on the card say things like which website names it covers and whether its owner may stamp other cards.

references.text: Cooper, D., et al., "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile", RFC 5280, May 2008.
Housley, R., et al., "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile", RFC 3280, April 2002.

summary: RFC 5280 profiles X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 certificate revocation lists for use on the Internet. It defines the certificate fields and extensions, how a relying party validates a certification path from a trust anchor, and how revocation is checked with CRLs.

eli5.summary: A certificate is an ID card for a website or person, stamped by someone everyone trusts. This RFC says what goes on the card and how to check the stamp is real.

tldr.problem: A client needs to know that a public key really belongs to the server it is talking to.
tldr.mechanism: A CA signs a certificate binding a name to a key; the client builds a chain of such certificates up to a trust anchor and checks signatures, validity dates, constraints and revocation status.
tldr.outcome: It is the basis of web PKI certificates for TLS, and it defines the exact fields and extensions that tooling parses.

questions: how does certificate path validation work
today: Every HTTPS site presents an X.509 certificate profiled by this RFC. Browsers and operating systems ship their own sets of trusted roots, and the Subject Alternative Name extension is what clients match against the host name. Revocation is often checked with OCSP (RFC 6960) as well as the CRLs this RFC defines.

data.title: Certificate (RFC 5280, section 4.1)
data.code:
Certificate  ::=  SEQUENCE  {
     tbsCertificate       TBSCertificate,
     signatureAlgorithm   AlgorithmIdentifier,
     signatureValue       BIT STRING  }

TBSCertificate  ::=  SEQUENCE  {
     version         [0]  EXPLICIT Version DEFAULT v1,
     serialNumber         CertificateSerialNumber,
     signature            AlgorithmIdentifier,
     issuer               Name,
     validity             Validity,
     subject              Name,
     subjectPublicKeyInfo SubjectPublicKeyInfo,
     issuerUniqueID  [1]  IMPLICIT UniqueIdentifier OPTIONAL,
     subjectUniqueID [2]  IMPLICIT UniqueIdentifier OPTIONAL,
     extensions      [3]  EXPLICIT Extensions OPTIONAL }
